medical.title: New guidelines released for care after head injury
medical.summary: New Scandinavian guidelines aim to support emergency care professionals in the assessment of adults with minimal, mild and moderate head injuries. Based on a broad review of the evidence, the guidelines include a more individualized approach to head computed tomography and in-hospital observation. The study was led by researchers at several departments, including Karolinska Institutet and Stockholm South General Hospital and is published in The Lancet Regional Health—Europe.

medical.title: Blood sugar spikes: What actually works to manage them
medical.summary: Blood sugar, also called blood glucose, rises after eating. Seeing that rise on a wearable monitor can make an ordinary meal look worrying. But a higher reading after lunch does not, by itself, mean that something has gone wrong.

medical.title: Patient age may shape which mutations drive melanoma
medical.summary: Precision medicine for cancer seeks to match treatment to the genetic changes found in a patient's tumor. A new Yale study suggests that for melanoma there may be an important clue to consider: the patient's age.

medical.title: Why the doomsday prediction of 1960 matters today
medical.summary: According to the late Heinz von Foerster, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, is doomsday. Professor von Foerster and two colleagues at the University of Illinois published that prediction in 1960 in the respected journal Science. The paper has been widely discussed ever since.

medical.title: New clinical definition outperforms BMI in diagnosing obesity
medical.summary: A new diagnostic definition of obesity outperforms body mass index (BMI) in identifying differences in health and prognosis, including mortality risk, according to a large international study published in Nature.

medical.title: 'Fossil record' in stored blood samples lets scientists trace leukemia back decades before diagnosis
medical.summary: Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over the decades before diagnosis, showing that in two-thirds of cases the first cancer-driving mutation had been acquired before the age of 20—more than 50 years before diagnosis.

medical.title: Receptor map uncovers hidden sites that could guide asthma drug design
medical.summary: Researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) have developed a new way of identifying new druggable sites on a family of proteins that could help design treatments with fewer side effects for a very wide range of conditions from heart disease to depression.

medical.title: First atlas tracks proteins that cross the blood-brain barrier
medical.summary: Your brain is protected by the blood-brain barrier—a network of cells in the brain's blood vessels that serves as a border between the brain and the rest of your bloodstream. But it's not just a barrier; it's a sophisticated interface that shuttles specific molecules between the blood and the brain to keep your brain healthy.

medical.title: Human neurons regain communication in motor neuron disease lab models
medical.summary: A novel potential treatment approach for motor neuron disease (MND), similar to the approach being pursued with an investigational drug that recently entered human clinical trials, has been shown to restore broken communication between neurons in lab models of the disease. This could have beneficial therapeutic implications for 97% of people with MND, for whom there is currently no significant disease-modifying treatment.

medical.title: Molecular brace traps two cancer-driving proteins to suppress prostate cancer growth in preclinical tests
medical.summary: Many modern cancer drugs typically target a specific protein or signaling pathway to treat tumors. Now, researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center are taking a new approach by throwing a molecular wrench into the machinery driving prostate cancer. In preclinical studies, this new approach demonstrated greater antitumor activity while sparing normal cells.

medical.title: Three brain biotypes found in study of kids with ADHD, anxiety
medical.summary: Three distinct brain biotypes exist in children who have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorder or both, a new Stanford Medicine–led study has shown. The discovery could help clarify a confusing picture of two of the most common mental health conditions of childhood, which often overlap. Each biotype is characterized by malfunctions in a specific set of brain circuits, according to the study, published in Nature Mental Health.

medical.title: Sore throats help inform Strep A vaccine trials
medical.summary: One in seven children develops a sore throat caused by Strep A bacteria every year, according to a new study that will help inform future vaccine trials.

medical.title: Even substitute PFAS cause metabolic stress in zebrafish embryos
medical.summary: Publishing in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, researchers from Kyushu University used zebrafish embryos to study the health effects of the PFAS called PFBS (perfluorobutanesulfonic acid), a substitute PFAS thought to be safer than traditional compounds. They found that while PFBS did not generate any obvious external dysfunction, the compound still gets absorbed and accumulates in the zebrafish embryo. Results showed that PFBS caused disruptions in the metabolic pathways for sugars and fat, which led to oxidative stress. Embryos also showed physical impairments in heart function, facial development, nervous system development and visual response.

medical.title: Office lighting experiments raise questions about human health
medical.summary: If you spend your workday under fluorescent lights, new research from Michigan State University suggests your body may notice. In a study of animals that, like people, are active during the day, researchers found that living under fluorescent office lighting was linked to weaker daily rhythms, higher rates of diabetic-range blood glucose and less active sperm compared with living under daylight-equivalent light. But a single hour of midday light helped make up the difference.

medical.title: Study finds gradebook data can help predict risk of drug use in adolescents
medical.summary: GPA has long been a benchmark for measuring success in students. It can also do more than indicate academic accomplishment: Health studies have established a strong correlation between GPA and the risk of unhealthy behaviors in adolescents, including substance abuse.

medical.title: Lifetime trauma linked to dementia and memory problems in older Australians, study
medical.summary: The study of more than 1,800 older Australians found that people who had experienced lifetime trauma were more likely to have mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and performed worse on working memory and executive function tests.

medical.title: The history and future of neuroeconomics: Q&A
medical.summary: So, what exactly is neuroeconomics? The Society for Neuroeconomics website describes it as a field that "represents the confluence of economics, psychology, and neuroscience in the study of human decision making." But for Antonio Rangel (BS '93), Caltech's Bing professor of neuroscience, behavioral biology and economics and past president of the Society for Neuroeconomics, the aim of the field is much more profound.

medical.title: A gut microbe shields mice from Parkinson's-like brain damage
medical.summary: Parkinson's disease is usually thought of as a brain disease, but many patients notice gut trouble—constipation above all—years or even decades before their hands begin to tremble. That timing has led researchers to ask whether the illness sometimes begins in the intestine, and whether treating the gut early could change what later happens in the brain.

medical.title: Common skin cancer rising faster in women
medical.summary: New research led by QIMR Berghofer has uncovered a decades-long increase in the rates of a common form of skin cancer across Australia and Europe, highlighting a growing but underrecognized public health challenge.

medical.title: Canine companionship, with a catch: Health effects of big-city dog ownership differ by location
medical.summary: How neighborhoods support healthy aging is a key question for aging societies. Yet little is known about how dog walking, an everyday activity, interacts with the neighborhood environment in dense Asian cities.

medical.title: Stress more strongly linked to poorer quality of life among adults with multiple chronic conditions
medical.summary: Perceived stress is more strongly associated with poorer health-related quality of life among adults living with two or more chronic conditions than among those without chronic conditions, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland.

medical.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
medical.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

medical.title: America's long-term care system needs help: Can Europe provide a model for how to improve it?
medical.summary: For millions of Americans, long-term care presents enormous financial, logistical and emotional challenges. Private long-term care insurance is prohibitively expensive or simply unavailable, and most older Americans aren't eligible for Medicaid until they exhaust nearly all their financial resources.

medical.title: Caitlin Moran on how to find hope when the world feels hopeless
medical.summary: The journalist and author reflects on a year spent challenging her own pessimism – and on why small actions can make a big difference The post Caitlin Moran on how to find hope when the world feels hopeless appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Effective obesity treatments reach few eligible teens, study finds
medical.summary: Despite the arrival of powerful new anti-obesity medications and growing evidence supporting weight-loss surgery for adolescents, the vast majority of eligible teens are receiving neither treatment, according to a new study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in JAMA Pediatrics.

science.title: A gold–copper strategy for building interlocked nitrogen-doped carbon nanohoops
science.summary: Catenanes are molecules in which two or more rings are mechanically interlocked like the links of a chain, without any chemical bonds between them. Since Jean-Pierre Sauvage, who later shared the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, reported an efficient metal-templated synthesis in 1983, catenanes have attracted attention as fundamental frameworks for molecular machines.

science.title: About 15,000 land vertebrate species could lose habitat to sea-level rise by 2100
science.summary: The rate of sea-level rise is now more than 4 millimeters (0.16 inches) per year, having more than doubled since 1993–2002. Scientists estimate that this figure may go up to 10 millimeters (0.39 inches) per year in the near future. The inundation of coastlines and islands will affect human and animal habitats alike.

science.title: Plants feel the heat: How a protein 'thermometer' helps plants adapt to climate
science.summary: Plants continuously adapt to environmental changes, and temperature is a key signal for growth and flowering. How plant thermometers, or "thermosensors," work at the molecular level is not well understood.

science.title: Nuclear softening at an embryo's two-cell stage may be vital for further embryonic development
science.summary: A research team led by Kyushu University and the National Institute of Genetics has discovered that during the two-cell stage of mouse embryonic development, the embryo's nucleus softens and deforms. This nuclear softening is an integral part of major zygotic gene activation, where approximately 2,000 genes necessary for embryonic development activate simultaneously. This indicates that nuclear softening is a critical step for further embryonic development.

science.title: New review explores how faint 'glow' from plants could transform global monitoring of photosynthesis
science.summary: A faint glow emitted by plants as they absorb sunlight could offer scientists a powerful new way to monitor photosynthesis across the planet. Fully realizing that potential, however, will require advances in both the general understanding of plant biology and the satellite technology used to observe it.

science.title: New gas sensor detects liver disease–related compounds in breath
science.summary: Researchers have recently developed a gas sensor that can detect tiny amounts of dimethyl sulfide in human breath, even in the presence of interfering gases and high humidity. The study was carried out by researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with the Key Laboratory of Odor Pollution Control of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and Shenzhen Technology University.

science.title: 11,000-year-old clay fragments reveal early experiments in pottery-making
science.summary: Long before pottery became commonplace in Southwest Asia, people living beside the Upper Tigris were experimenting with ways to turn clay into containers.

science.title: Crushes and other injuries: What science tells us about grieving a heartbreak
science.summary: Something funny happened at work, and there is one person you really want to tell. You stare at their name in your contact list. You know that if you call, no one will answer. They're gone.

science.title: Beyond food: Bran-based gels show potential for targeted drug delivery
science.summary: When it comes to colon health, the benefits of wheat and rye bran in whole-grain foods are well known. Now researchers in Sweden have shown how these fibers may have a therapeutic use, too. A new study published in the journal Biomacromolecules demonstrates the potential to use bran fiber for direct delivery of drugs to treat colon diseases like ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or colorectal cancer.

science.title: Glass does surprising things when stretched 1 atom wide. The discovery could help shrink electronics
science.summary: Smartwatches worn on millions of wrists today pack vastly more processing power than the computers that helped Apollo astronauts land on the moon. But the scientific drive to go tiny has come at a cost: It means heat, electricity and energy now have much less room to flow through devices.

science.title: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests unexpected origins for organics in space
science.summary: Samples from the Bennu asteroid, which is currently more than 200 million miles (322 million kilometers) from Earth, and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969, both contain molecules that build proteins necessary for life. New research has found that the molecules may have formed through the same process but originated far from one another in the solar system.

science.title: New strategy boosts iron-based single-atom catalysts for Fenton-like reactions
science.summary: Researchers at the Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry (XTIPC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a core-shell confined iron-based single-atom catalyst that combines high Fenton-like catalytic activity with structural stability, enabling nearly complete removal of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) within 20 minutes under mildly acidic conditions.

science.title: The faces of iridium: One metal, many reactions
science.summary: The same metal can have many faces, and each tells a different chemical story. At the atomic scale, those different faces can push the same reaction along very different paths.

science.title: III-nitride device integrates sensing and memory for in-sensor computing
science.summary: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C.

science.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
science.summary: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside.

science.title: New algorithm improves phase readout for space-based gravitational wave detection
science.summary: In a study published in Optics Communications, a research group led by Yu Tao from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences proposed a new analytical phase readout algorithm for deep frequency modulation interferometry (DFMI).

science.title: Wonder and ore: A spectacular new view from space maps Australia's mineral wealth
science.summary: A new tool that uses detailed satellite images to help unlock Australia's mineral wealth has been unveiled.

science.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
science.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

science.title: Research snapshot: The use of icons in aphasia-friendly texts
science.summary: Pictorial reading supports, such as icons, can help people with aphasia better comprehend the material and enjoy the reading process. But exactly what type of icon is most helpful?

science.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
science.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

science.title: Roman-era 'frog feast' near Cambridge was the work of owls, bone analysis suggests
science.summary: Around 1,800 years ago, over 9,000 bones, mainly from frogs, ended up in an Iron Age/Roman gully near Cambridge. When archaeologists first dug them up, speculation soon followed. Were these the remains of a Roman frog feast or perhaps the skeletal aftermath of a ritual?

science.title: Finding new life in old chemicals for pharmaceuticals using light-driven chemistry
science.summary: Drug companies maintain large libraries of chemical compounds that can be screened for potential use in the development of new pharmaceuticals. One class of these compounds, sulfonamides, is used in antibiotics and in drugs to treat type 2 diabetes, hypertension and inflammation. Thousands of these sulfonamides exist in these libraries, but their use beyond their initial purpose is limited because they are difficult to chemically modify.

science.title: Deeper dives are linked to longer surface recovery in sea lions
science.summary: Sea lions, marine mammals belonging to the eared seal family, have to dive to search for food and other resources. Between dives, however, they return to the surface to breathe and recover.

science.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
science.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

science.title: Why land—a scarce resource—is so important for climate protection
science.summary: A new study quantifies, for the first time, the interrelationships and competing objectives of two major areas of action for reducing greenhouse gas emissions: the phaseout of fossil fuels and measures taken on natural land, such as farmland, forests and wetlands. It demonstrates how a well-balanced policy mix can keep costs low for both people and nature. The study, conducted at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), was published in Nature Sustainability.

environment.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
environment.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

environment.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
environment.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

environment.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
environment.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

environment.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
environment.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

environment.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
environment.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

environment.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
environment.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.title: Studiu Oxford: zeci de decese ale străinilor aflați în detenție în Grecia nu apar în statisticile oficiale ale poliției
mix_items.summary: Peste 100 de cetățeni străini au decedat începând din anul 2000 în secțiile de poliție sau în centrele pentru migranți din Grecia, care dispun de facilități medicale inadecvate, inclusiv 34 de decese care nu au fost înregistrate oficial, potrivit unui studiu publicat marți de cercetătorii de la Universitatea Oxford, citat de Reuters.

mix_items.title: Tehnica ganglionului santinelă: o procedură care poate schimba abordarea chirurgicală în cancerul de sân
mix_items.summary: n fazele incipiente ale cancerului de sân, atunci când boala este depistată precoce sau când caracteristicile tumorii maligne o permit, abordarea chirurgicală se poate restrânge la scoaterea ganglionului santinelă, primul invadat de celulele canceroase din tumora aflată în sân. Prin injectarea unui substanţe radioactive, medicul va putea observa gradul de invadare şi va putea decide cea mai potrivită terapie.

mix_items.title: Medicina modernă, mai aproape de pacienți. Cum schimbă clinicile multidisciplinare accesul la servicii medicale în orașele din România
mix_items.summary: Accesul la servicii medicale specializate nu mai trebuie să presupună, în toate situațiile, deplasarea către marile centre universitare. Dezvoltarea clinicilor private multidisciplinare din orașele regionale oferă pacienților posibilitatea de a beneficia de consultații, investigații și tratamente complexe mai aproape de casă. mix_items.summary: Fețe plouate în studio la România TV, după atentatul din Cracovia. mix_items.title: A gold–copper strategy for building interlocked nitrogen-doped carbon nanohoops
mix_items.summary: Catenanes are molecules in which two or more rings are mechanically interlocked like the links of a chain, without any chemical bonds between them. Since Jean-Pierre Sauvage, who later shared the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, reported an efficient metal-templated synthesis in 1983, catenanes have attracted attention as fundamental frameworks for molecular machines.

mix_items.title: New guidelines released for care after head injury
mix_items.summary: New Scandinavian guidelines aim to support emergency care professionals in the assessment of adults with minimal, mild and moderate head injuries. Based on a broad review of the evidence, the guidelines include a more individualized approach to head computed tomography and in-hospital observation. The study was led by researchers at several departments, including Karolinska Institutet and Stockholm South General Hospital and is published in The Lancet Regional Health—Europe.

mix_items.title: About 15,000 land vertebrate species could lose habitat to sea-level rise by 2100
mix_items.summary: The rate of sea-level rise is now more than 4 millimeters (0.16 inches) per year, having more than doubled since 1993–2002. Scientists estimate that this figure may go up to 10 millimeters (0.39 inches) per year in the near future. The inundation of coastlines and islands will affect human and animal habitats alike.

mix_items.title: Blood sugar spikes: What actually works to manage them
mix_items.summary: Blood sugar, also called blood glucose, rises after eating. Seeing that rise on a wearable monitor can make an ordinary meal look worrying. But a higher reading after lunch does not, by itself, mean that something has gone wrong.

mix_items.title: Patient age may shape which mutations drive melanoma
mix_items.summary: Precision medicine for cancer seeks to match treatment to the genetic changes found in a patient's tumor. A new Yale study suggests that for melanoma there may be an important clue to consider: the patient's age.

mix_items.title: Plants feel the heat: How a protein 'thermometer' helps plants adapt to climate
mix_items.summary: Plants continuously adapt to environmental changes, and temperature is a key signal for growth and flowering. How plant thermometers, or "thermosensors," work at the molecular level is not well understood.

mix_items.title: Why the doomsday prediction of 1960 matters today
mix_items.summary: According to the late Heinz von Foerster, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, is doomsday. Professor von Foerster and two colleagues at the University of Illinois published that prediction in 1960 in the respected journal Science. The paper has been widely discussed ever since.

mix_items.title: Nuclear softening at an embryo's two-cell stage may be vital for further embryonic development
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Kyushu University and the National Institute of Genetics has discovered that during the two-cell stage of mouse embryonic development, the embryo's nucleus softens and deforms. This nuclear softening is an integral part of major zygotic gene activation, where approximately 2,000 genes necessary for embryonic development activate simultaneously. This indicates that nuclear softening is a critical step for further embryonic development.

mix_items.title: New clinical definition outperforms BMI in diagnosing obesity
mix_items.summary: A new diagnostic definition of obesity outperforms body mass index (BMI) in identifying differences in health and prognosis, including mortality risk, according to a large international study published in Nature.

mix_items.title: 'Fossil record' in stored blood samples lets scientists trace leukemia back decades before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over the decades before diagnosis, showing that in two-thirds of cases the first cancer-driving mutation had been acquired before the age of 20—more than 50 years before diagnosis.

mix_items.title: Receptor map uncovers hidden sites that could guide asthma drug design
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) have developed a new way of identifying new druggable sites on a family of proteins that could help design treatments with fewer side effects for a very wide range of conditions from heart disease to depression.

mix_items.title: First atlas tracks proteins that cross the blood-brain barrier
mix_items.summary: Your brain is protected by the blood-brain barrier—a network of cells in the brain's blood vessels that serves as a border between the brain and the rest of your bloodstream. But it's not just a barrier; it's a sophisticated interface that shuttles specific molecules between the blood and the brain to keep your brain healthy.

mix_items.title: Human neurons regain communication in motor neuron disease lab models
mix_items.summary: A novel potential treatment approach for motor neuron disease (MND), similar to the approach being pursued with an investigational drug that recently entered human clinical trials, has been shown to restore broken communication between neurons in lab models of the disease. This could have beneficial therapeutic implications for 97% of people with MND, for whom there is currently no significant disease-modifying treatment.

mix_items.title: New review explores how faint 'glow' from plants could transform global monitoring of photosynthesis
mix_items.summary: A faint glow emitted by plants as they absorb sunlight could offer scientists a powerful new way to monitor photosynthesis across the planet. Fully realizing that potential, however, will require advances in both the general understanding of plant biology and the satellite technology used to observe it.

mix_items.title: Molecular brace traps two cancer-driving proteins to suppress prostate cancer growth in preclinical tests
mix_items.summary: Many modern cancer drugs typically target a specific protein or signaling pathway to treat tumors. Now, researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center are taking a new approach by throwing a molecular wrench into the machinery driving prostate cancer. In preclinical studies, this new approach demonstrated greater antitumor activity while sparing normal cells.

mix_items.title: Three brain biotypes found in study of kids with ADHD, anxiety
mix_items.summary: Three distinct brain biotypes exist in children who have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorder or both, a new Stanford Medicine–led study has shown. The discovery could help clarify a confusing picture of two of the most common mental health conditions of childhood, which often overlap. Each biotype is characterized by malfunctions in a specific set of brain circuits, according to the study, published in Nature Mental Health.

mix_items.title: New gas sensor detects liver disease–related compounds in breath
mix_items.summary: Researchers have recently developed a gas sensor that can detect tiny amounts of dimethyl sulfide in human breath, even in the presence of interfering gases and high humidity. The study was carried out by researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with the Key Laboratory of Odor Pollution Control of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and Shenzhen Technology University.

mix_items.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
mix_items.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

mix_items.title: 11,000-year-old clay fragments reveal early experiments in pottery-making
mix_items.summary: Long before pottery became commonplace in Southwest Asia, people living beside the Upper Tigris were experimenting with ways to turn clay into containers.

mix_items.title: Sore throats help inform Strep A vaccine trials
mix_items.summary: One in seven children develops a sore throat caused by Strep A bacteria every year, according to a new study that will help inform future vaccine trials.

mix_items.title: Crushes and other injuries: What science tells us about grieving a heartbreak
mix_items.summary: Something funny happened at work, and there is one person you really want to tell. You stare at their name in your contact list. You know that if you call, no one will answer. They're gone.

mix_items.title: Beyond food: Bran-based gels show potential for targeted drug delivery
mix_items.summary: When it comes to colon health, the benefits of wheat and rye bran in whole-grain foods are well known. Now researchers in Sweden have shown how these fibers may have a therapeutic use, too. A new study published in the journal Biomacromolecules demonstrates the potential to use bran fiber for direct delivery of drugs to treat colon diseases like ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or colorectal cancer.

mix_items.title: Even substitute PFAS cause metabolic stress in zebrafish embryos
mix_items.summary: Publishing in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, researchers from Kyushu University used zebrafish embryos to study the health effects of the PFAS called PFBS (perfluorobutanesulfonic acid), a substitute PFAS thought to be safer than traditional compounds. They found that while PFBS did not generate any obvious external dysfunction, the compound still gets absorbed and accumulates in the zebrafish embryo. Results showed that PFBS caused disruptions in the metabolic pathways for sugars and fat, which led to oxidative stress. Embryos also showed physical impairments in heart function, facial development, nervous system development and visual response.

mix_items.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
mix_items.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

mix_items.title: Office lighting experiments raise questions about human health
mix_items.summary: If you spend your workday under fluorescent lights, new research from Michigan State University suggests your body may notice. In a study of animals that, like people, are active during the day, researchers found that living under fluorescent office lighting was linked to weaker daily rhythms, higher rates of diabetic-range blood glucose and less active sperm compared with living under daylight-equivalent light. But a single hour of midday light helped make up the difference.

mix_items.title: Glass does surprising things when stretched 1 atom wide. The discovery could help shrink electronics
mix_items.summary: Smartwatches worn on millions of wrists today pack vastly more processing power than the computers that helped Apollo astronauts land on the moon. But the scientific drive to go tiny has come at a cost: It means heat, electricity and energy now have much less room to flow through devices.

mix_items.title: Study finds gradebook data can help predict risk of drug use in adolescents
mix_items.summary: GPA has long been a benchmark for measuring success in students. It can also do more than indicate academic accomplishment: Health studies have established a strong correlation between GPA and the risk of unhealthy behaviors in adolescents, including substance abuse.

mix_items.title: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests unexpected origins for organics in space
mix_items.summary: Samples from the Bennu asteroid, which is currently more than 200 million miles (322 million kilometers) from Earth, and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969, both contain molecules that build proteins necessary for life. New research has found that the molecules may have formed through the same process but originated far from one another in the solar system.

mix_items.title: Lifetime trauma linked to dementia and memory problems in older Australians, study
mix_items.summary: The study of more than 1,800 older Australians found that people who had experienced lifetime trauma were more likely to have mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and performed worse on working memory and executive function tests.

mix_items.title: The history and future of neuroeconomics: Q&A
mix_items.summary: So, what exactly is neuroeconomics? The Society for Neuroeconomics website describes it as a field that "represents the confluence of economics, psychology, and neuroscience in the study of human decision making." But for Antonio Rangel (BS '93), Caltech's Bing professor of neuroscience, behavioral biology and economics and past president of the Society for Neuroeconomics, the aim of the field is much more profound.

mix_items.title: A gut microbe shields mice from Parkinson's-like brain damage
mix_items.summary: Parkinson's disease is usually thought of as a brain disease, but many patients notice gut trouble—constipation above all—years or even decades before their hands begin to tremble. That timing has led researchers to ask whether the illness sometimes begins in the intestine, and whether treating the gut early could change what later happens in the brain.

mix_items.title: New strategy boosts iron-based single-atom catalysts for Fenton-like reactions
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry (XTIPC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a core-shell confined iron-based single-atom catalyst that combines high Fenton-like catalytic activity with structural stability, enabling nearly complete removal of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) within 20 minutes under mildly acidic conditions.

mix_items.title: The faces of iridium: One metal, many reactions
mix_items.summary: The same metal can have many faces, and each tells a different chemical story. At the atomic scale, those different faces can push the same reaction along very different paths.

mix_items.title: III-nitride device integrates sensing and memory for in-sensor computing
mix_items.summary: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C.

mix_items.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
mix_items.summary: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside.

mix_items.title: Common skin cancer rising faster in women
mix_items.summary: New research led by QIMR Berghofer has uncovered a decades-long increase in the rates of a common form of skin cancer across Australia and Europe, highlighting a growing but underrecognized public health challenge.

mix_items.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
mix_items.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

mix_items.title: New algorithm improves phase readout for space-based gravitational wave detection
mix_items.summary: In a study published in Optics Communications, a research group led by Yu Tao from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences proposed a new analytical phase readout algorithm for deep frequency modulation interferometry (DFMI).

mix_items.title: Canine companionship, with a catch: Health effects of big-city dog ownership differ by location
mix_items.summary: How neighborhoods support healthy aging is a key question for aging societies. Yet little is known about how dog walking, an everyday activity, interacts with the neighborhood environment in dense Asian cities.

mix_items.title: Wonder and ore: A spectacular new view from space maps Australia's mineral wealth
mix_items.summary: A new tool that uses detailed satellite images to help unlock Australia's mineral wealth has been unveiled.

mix_items.title: Stress more strongly linked to poorer quality of life among adults with multiple chronic conditions
mix_items.summary: Perceived stress is more strongly associated with poorer health-related quality of life among adults living with two or more chronic conditions than among those without chronic conditions, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland.

mix_items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
mix_items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

mix_items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

mix_items.title: Research snapshot: The use of icons in aphasia-friendly texts
mix_items.summary: Pictorial reading supports, such as icons, can help people with aphasia better comprehend the material and enjoy the reading process. But exactly what type of icon is most helpful?

mix_items.title: America's long-term care system needs help: Can Europe provide a model for how to improve it?
mix_items.summary: For millions of Americans, long-term care presents enormous financial, logistical and emotional challenges. Private long-term care insurance is prohibitively expensive or simply unavailable, and most older Americans aren't eligible for Medicaid until they exhaust nearly all their financial resources.

mix_items.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
mix_items.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

mix_items.title: Caitlin Moran on how to find hope when the world feels hopeless
mix_items.summary: The journalist and author reflects on a year spent challenging her own pessimism – and on why small actions can make a big difference The post Caitlin Moran on how to find hope when the world feels hopeless appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
mix_items.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

mix_items.title: Effective obesity treatments reach few eligible teens, study finds
mix_items.summary: Despite the arrival of powerful new anti-obesity medications and growing evidence supporting weight-loss surgery for adolescents, the vast majority of eligible teens are receiving neither treatment, according to a new study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in JAMA Pediatrics.

mix_items.title: Roman-era 'frog feast' near Cambridge was the work of owls, bone analysis suggests
mix_items.summary: Around 1,800 years ago, over 9,000 bones, mainly from frogs, ended up in an Iron Age/Roman gully near Cambridge. When archaeologists first dug them up, speculation soon followed. Were these the remains of a Roman frog feast or perhaps the skeletal aftermath of a ritual?

mix_items.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
mix_items.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

mix_items.title: Finding new life in old chemicals for pharmaceuticals using light-driven chemistry
mix_items.summary: Drug companies maintain large libraries of chemical compounds that can be screened for potential use in the development of new pharmaceuticals. One class of these compounds, sulfonamides, is used in antibiotics and in drugs to treat type 2 diabetes, hypertension and inflammation. Thousands of these sulfonamides exist in these libraries, but their use beyond their initial purpose is limited because they are difficult to chemically modify.

mix_items.title: Deeper dives are linked to longer surface recovery in sea lions
mix_items.summary: Sea lions, marine mammals belonging to the eared seal family, have to dive to search for food and other resources. Between dives, however, they return to the surface to breathe and recover.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
mix_items.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

mix_items.title: Why land—a scarce resource—is so important for climate protection
mix_items.summary: A new study quantifies, for the first time, the interrelationships and competing objectives of two major areas of action for reducing greenhouse gas emissions: the phaseout of fossil fuels and measures taken on natural land, such as farmland, forests and wetlands. It demonstrates how a well-balanced policy mix can keep costs low for both people and nature. The study, conducted at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), was published in Nature Sustainability.

mix_items.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
